note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; code is spelled the way it is said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: The last reel proved that append is big O of one, amortized.
Now put the vector behind a service.
Each request appends one key. One tick is the time to write one element, and a request arrives every four ticks.
This is a model of a service, not a measurement.
The append that finds it full, number five hundred twenty four thousand, two hundred eighty nine, copies every key before it.
While it runs, one hundred thirty one thousand, seventy two requests arrive. They all wait.
Is this service fast?
Percentiles describe a tail.

P fifty is the median. The ninety ninth percentile, p ninety nine, is the cost that ninety nine of every hundred appends stay at or under. For p ninety nine point nine, it is nine hundred ninety nine of every thousand.
Of a million appends to the doubling vector, twenty resize. The largest copies about five hundred twenty four thousand keys.
What is the p ninety nine cost of an append?
answer: One write.
Only twenty of a million appends resize. That is two thousandths of a percent.
So p fifty, p ninety nine, p ninety nine point nine, and even p ninety nine point nine nine are all one write.
The mean is about two, and the maximum is five hundred twenty four thousand, two hundred eighty nine.
Doubling does not hurt the p ninety nine of the appends themselves. The harm is in everything that waits, behind the one rare spike.

lines: Per append, the tail is one write.
Per request, with the wait included, p ninety nine is four hundred ninety four thousand, two hundred eighty nine ticks.
Three hundred forty nine thousand, five hundred fifteen requests wait behind a resize. That is thirty five percent.
A service is judged on its requests. So their tail is the one that counts.
The copy is one append. The wait is everyone's.
Fan out multiplies the tail.
Dean and Barroso give an example. A server answers in ten milliseconds, but takes a full second at its p ninety nine.
A request served by one such server is slow one time in a hundred.
Now take a request that has to wait for a hundred of them. It is slow, sixty three percent of the time.
A tail that you can safely ignore, on each single server, is the common case for a whole request.
With two thousand servers, and one in ten thousand slow, it is almost one request in five.
Accounting charged three per append. One to write, two saved.
Deamortization spends the two right away.
When the vector of eight fills, append nine allocates sixteen slots, and moves two old keys.
The gauge of keys left to copy drains from eight down to zero, by two on each of the appends, nine to twelve.
Over sixteen appends, both vectors write thirty one elements.
But no append costs more than three. The dashed line is now a worst case bound.
Here is the state after append ten.
The old buffer. The new one. The count n. And the frontier k: how many old keys have moved.
An append writes its key at slot n of the new buffer, then moves the next two old keys.
A read at index i uses the old buffer only if k is at most i, and i is below m, the old key count.
Everything else is in the new buffer. One comparison picks the buffer.
Append nine allocated sixteen slots and moved two old keys. Six are left to copy, and seven slots are free.
Every later append writes one new key and moves two old ones.
How many of the sixteen slots are in use when the last old key moves?
answer: Twelve.
Appends nine to twelve move two keys each, eight in all, while n goes from eight to twelve.
The copying finishes when the element count reaches one and a half times the previous capacity, leaving twenty five percent of the new buffer unused.
Moving one key per append would also finish, but exactly as the buffer fills, with no slack.
For growth factor g, move at least one over g minus one keys per append.

lines: Same total writes. A different bill.

Both buffers stay alive while the copy runs. At the last resize of a million appends, that is the same twelve mebibytes of peak as plain doubling, but held for about a quarter of a million appends, not one.
Every read pays a comparison with the frontier.
More than half the appends now cost three, so the median got worse.
And the big O of one worst case assumes that allocating a buffer is big O of one.
A second structure, apart from arrays that grow.
Global rebuilding: let a structure go stale, then rebuild all of it.
A sorted vector deletes by leaving a tombstone. A lookup reports a tombstoned key as absent.
Once half the slots are tombstones, copy the live keys into a compact vector.
That costs theta of n, after theta of n deletes. So it is big O of one, amortized.
The doubling vector does the very same thing, for growth.
And at about a million keys, one delete still copies half a million.
Overmars's global rebuilding goes further. Start early, and rebuild while serving.
At four tombstones of sixteen, begin a new copy.
Each delete also scans eight slots of the old copy, and copies the live keys. Queries still use the old copy.
A key deleted after it was copied goes into a log. The log is replayed before the swap.
Eight slots a delete finish the copy before the old one is half tombstones. The vector's deadline again.
No delete writes more than ten.
Now a tree where only a part goes bad.
A scapegoat tree is a plain binary search tree. Each node holds a key and two pointers, nothing else.
The root keeps two counts: the size, and the largest size since the last full rebuild.
Fix alpha strictly between one half and one. Here, alpha is two thirds. It is a balance parameter, not the last reel's load factor.
A node deeper than h of n, the floor of log base one point five of n, is too deep. Here n counts the new node.
Inserting sixty nine lands at depth six, below the limit of five.
Climb from sixty nine, the deep node.
At each ancestor, compare its heavier child's subtree with the ancestor's own subtree.
The scapegoat is the first ancestor where that child holds more than alpha, two thirds.
Which node is it?
answer: Eighty seven.
From sixty nine going up: sixty three's heavier child holds one of its two nodes. Eighty's holds two of three. Exactly two thirds is still allowed.
Fifty four's holds three of five. That is under two thirds, though it looks lopsided.
Eighty seven's left child holds five of its six nodes. That is over two thirds, so eighty seven is the scapegoat.
The sizes are counted on the way up. No node stores one.

lines: Rebuild the scapegoat's subtree, perfectly balanced.
Walk its six nodes in order. Make the lower middle one, sixty three, the root. Then recurse.
The time is proportional to the subtree.
Who pays? Each node holds a constant times the difference between its left and right sizes, as potential.
An insert adds a little at each of its big O of log n ancestors, and an unbalanced node holds theta of its own size. That is enough for the climb, and for the rebuild.
So inserts cost big O of log n, amortized.
Deletes never push a node deeper. But they shrink n, so the tree grows tall for its size.
The root's second count handles this. When the size drops below alpha times the largest size, rebuild the whole tree.
That is global rebuilding again, inside the scapegoat tree.
It takes theta of n deletes first. At a million keys, delete three hundred thirty three thousand, three hundred thirty four rebuilds six hundred sixty six thousand, six hundred sixty six nodes.
Be honest about the tree. It is amortized, not deamortized.
Big O of log n per insert, over any sequence. But one insert can rebuild most of the tree.
A million increasing keys cost twenty eight writes per insert on average. The p ninety nine is two hundred forty six.
One insert, near the nine hundred thousandth, rebuilds about three quarters of a million nodes.
Searches never restructure anything. Their worst case stays big O of log n, and the depth is at most thirty four here.
Back to the service.
With two moves per append, no append takes more than three ticks. Requests arrive four apart. So no queue ever forms.
Request p ninety nine and the maximum are three ticks, against more than four hundred ninety thousand before.
The total writes are the same. The median rose from one to three.
And every tick charged a write the same, wherever in memory it landed.
The vector holds one million, forty eight thousand, five hundred seventy six keys, and is full.
With incremental copying at two keys per append, for how many appends are both buffers alive?
And what does the costliest append write?
answer: Five hundred twenty four thousand, two hundred eighty eight appends, and three writes.
The next append allocates twice the slots. Moving the keys at two per append then takes five hundred twenty four thousand, two hundred eighty eight appends.
That ends when n is one million, five hundred seventy two thousand, eight hundred sixty four.
Meanwhile both buffers, twenty four mebibytes, stay alive.
Each of those appends writes its key and moves two.

lines: A teammate's get of i reads the new buffer, for every index, while a copy runs.
Right after append number nine, the old size is eight, and the frontier, k, is two.
What does get of five return?
answer: An empty slot.
Only indices below two have moved. New slots two to seven are still empty, and slot eight holds key nine.
Reads must check the frontier. Index i is in the old buffer if k is at most i, and i is below m. Otherwise, the read goes to the new buffer.
Writes need the same rule, or a later move overwrites the new value with the old one.

lines: A nightly batch job appends a billion keys to a vector. Only its total running time matters.
A reviewer asks you to switch to incremental copying. Do you agree?
answer: No.
Both vectors write about two point one billion elements.
The incremental one also pays a comparison on every read, and holds two buffers longer.
Its gain is the tail. In a batch, no request waits behind the one append that writes over half a billion.
Deamortize when something waits on single operations: requests, frames, or a fan out.
